'''John Arthur Woollam''' (born 10 August 1939) is an American educator, research physicist, electrical engineer, and George Holmes Distinguished Professor at the [[University of Nebraska–Lincoln]] in [[Lincoln, Nebraska]]. He is also a successful entrepreneur who in 1987 founded the J.A. Woollam Company, an [[ellipsometry]] company based in Lincoln, Nebraska, and a world leader in the research, development, and commercialization of [[Ellipsometer|ellipsometry instruments]]. Woollam is also known as a philanthropist<ref>[http://landtrust.org/Stories/woollam.htm Creating Waves of Conservation: John Woollam] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120710221241/http://landtrust.org/Stories/woollam.htm |date=2012-07-10 }}. landtrust.org</ref> and nature conservationist.<ref>[http://www.nature.org/about-us/campaignforasustainableplanet/donors/john-woollam.xml Donors Making a Difference: John Woollam | The Nature Conservancy] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140812061845/http://www.nature.org/about-us/campaignforasustainableplanet/donors/john-woollam.xml |date=2014-08-12 }}. Nature.org. Retrieved on 2013-05-26.</ref>

==Early life and education==

John Woollam was born in [[Kalamazoo, Michigan]]. His interest in physics, engineering, and business was stimulated by his father, Arthur E. Woollam, who ran a water pump company in Kalamazoo. As a teenager John was not interested very much in school classes, but he spent hours at his father's company studying and building pumps. This attitude changed when he attended [[Kenyon College]] in [[Gambier, Ohio]], where he majored in physics. He earned his master's degree in 1963 and defended a Ph.D. in 1967 at the [[Michigan State University]].<ref name="phd">
{{cite thesis |type=PhD |publisher=Michigan State University |publication-place= |last=Woollam |first=John Arthur |date=1967 |title=Electron transport properties of metallic tin in high magnetic fields and at liquid helium temperatures |oclc=25904263 |hdl= |doi= |osti= |url=https://search.ebscohost.com/login.aspx?direct=true&db=cat09242a&AN=msuc.b24752514&site=eds-live&authtype=ip,guest&custid=s8364774&groupid=main&profile=eds }}
</ref> For 13 years after that, he was employed by [[NASA]] to work in [[cryophysics]], [[superconductivity]], and propulsion systems. While working at NASA, he earned a master's degree in electrical engineering from the Case Institute of Technology at [[Case Western Reserve University]] in [[Cleveland, Ohio]], in 1978.

==Career==

In 1979, John Woollam became a professor at the [[University of Nebraska–Lincoln]], taking over the laboratory and research group of retiring professor Nick Bashara, where he has researched the optical, electrical, and microstructural properties of solids and thin films as well as interfacial and environmental effects on materials.<ref name=unl-ece>{{Cite web|url=https://engineering.unl.edu/ece/faculty/john-woollam/|title = John Woollam &#124; College of Engineering &#124; University of Nebraska–Lincoln}}</ref> Trained as a solid-state experimental physicist, Woollam’s initial interest was in low-temperature physics, superconductors, and related materials;<ref>CW Chu, JA Woollam (Eds.), High Pressure and Low Temperature Physics, Plenum, New York (1978)</ref> however, in the 1980s he began to study [[Raman spectroscopy]]<ref>{{cite journal|doi=10.1103/PhysRevB.29.3482|title=Use of Raman scattering to investigate disorder and crystallite formation in as-deposited and annealed carbon films|year=1984|last1=Dillon|first1=R.|last2=Woollam|first2=John|last3=Katkanant|first3=V.|journal=Physical Review B|volume=29|issue=6|pages=3482|bibcode = 1984PhRvB..29.3482D }} This article has received 860+ citations in the [[Web of Science]] as of May 2013.</ref> and the optical characterization of surfaces and films of technological importance.<ref>{{cite journal|pmid=9992658|doi=10.1103/PhysRevB.40.5956|title=Optical-absorption edge and disorder effects in hydrogenated amorphous diamondlike carbon films|year=1989|last1=Datta|first1=T.|last2=Woollam|first2=John|last3=Notohamiprodjo|first3=W.|journal=Physical Review B|volume=40|issue=9|pages=5956–5960|bibcode = 1989PhRvB..40.5956D |url=http://digitalcommons.unl.edu/cgi/viewcontent.cgi?article=1074&context=electricalengineeringfacpub|url-access=subscription}}</ref> More recently, he has focused primarily on studying the development and application of [[ellipsometry]] to a wide range of materials, industrial,<ref>{{cite journal|doi=10.1063/1.1921336|title=Optical characterization of porous alumina from vacuum ultraviolet to midinfrared|year=2005|last1=Thompson|first1=Daniel W.|last2=Snyder|first2=Paul G.|last3=Castro|first3=Leon|last4=Yan|first4=Li|last5=Kaipa|first5=Prasuna|last6=Woollam|first6=John A.|journal=Journal of Applied Physics|volume=97|issue=11|pages=113511–113511–9|bibcode = 2005JAP....97k3511T |url=https://digitalcommons.unl.edu/electricalengineeringfacpub/6|url-access=subscription}}</ref> and biological<ref>{{cite journal|doi=10.1016/j.susc.2007.02.005|title=Repeatability of ellipsometric data in cholera toxin GM1–ELISA structures|year=2007|last1=Castro|first1=Leon G.|last2=Thompson|first2=Daniel W.|last3=Tiwald|first3=Thomas|last4=Berberov|first4=Emil M.|last5=Woollam|first5=John A.|journal=Surface Science|volume=601|issue=8|pages=1795|bibcode = 2007SurSc.601.1795C }}</ref> problems. Woollam and his group have contributed all over the world to the design, manufacture, and application of ellipsometric instruments at academic and corporate research/production facilities.

==J.A. Woollam Company==
In 1987, John Woollam founded the J.A. Woollam Company, an [[ellipsometry]] company located in [[Lincoln, Nebraska]].<ref>{{cite news|title=Lincoln company plans $20 million expansion in Haymarket|first=Matt|last=Olberding
|date=June 6, 2022|work=Lincoln Journal Star|access-date=August 9, 2022|url=https://journalstar.com/business/local/lincoln-company-plans-20-million-expansion-in-haymarket/article_57b7b1b0-939d-525d-aae4-adb3e12c56ca.amp.html}}</ref> The J.A. Woollam Company was originally founded as a spin-off of Woollam's research at the [[University of Nebraska–Lincoln]],<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.jawoollam.com/about-us|title = About Us}}</ref> but it has become a worldwide leader in the development and production of spectroscopic ellipsometers.

==Honors and awards==
*Winner of the 2017 R.F. Bunshah Award, where he presented the honorary lecture at the 2017 International Conference on Metallurgical Coatings and Thin Films (ICMCTF).<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://engineering.unl.edu/woollam-receive-icmctfs-rf-bunshah-award/|title=Woollam to receive ICMCTF's R.F. Bunshah Award &#124; College of Engineering &#124; University of Nebraska–Lincoln}}</ref>

*Fellow of the [[National Academy of Inventors]] (2014).<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://news.unl.edu/newsrooms/unltoday/article/woollam-named-national-academy-of-inventors-fellow/|title=Woollam named National Academy of Inventors Fellow|date=16 December 2014 }}</ref>

*Winner of the [[American Physical Society]]’s 2013 Industrial Applications of Physics prize for his sustained contributions in ellipsometry especially in extending the applications and in developing modern designs for these instruments.<ref>[http://www.aps.org/units/fiap/awards/recipient.cfm?first_nm=John&last_nm=Woollam&year=2013 APS Physics | FIAP | Recipient]. Aps.org (2012-09-21). Retrieved on 2013-05-26.</ref>

*Fellow at the [[American Vacuum Society]] (2006) 

*Honorary Doctorate (2004) [[Linkoping University]], Sweden.<ref name=unl-ece />

*Fellow at [[American Physical Society]] (1981) and a [[National Research Council (United States)|National Research Council]] Fellow (1967).<ref name=unl-ece />

*Among Woollam’s other successes are his former students. He has mentored many of them from their early undergraduate days through post-graduate education. Many of his former students have remained in the Midwest to form the talent base at the core of the J.A. Woollam Company.
